opus-5.5.text:
I think the difference is mostly about what you believe the bottleneck is.

The coding-agent approach says, roughly: AI research is a lot of engineering. Writing training code, running experiments, tuning hyperparameters, debugging, reading logs. If we can automate that loop with strong coding agents, we can run many more experiments in parallel, and progress speeds up. Eventually the agents improve the next generation of models, and you get a recursive loop. I think that's a reasonable bet, and a lot of what happens in AI labs really is engineering throughput. So I don't dismiss it at all.

My hesitation is that faster experiments don't automatically give you understanding. If the agent mostly does search, trying many things and keeping what improves a benchmark, you get a very efficient version of what the field already does: empirical trial and error. That can push the frontier, but it can also lock you into local optima. You optimize the transformer recipe more and more without asking whether there's a fundamentally better way to represent things.

What I care about is closer to "AI for the science of AI." Not just automating the engineer, but helping us find the principles. Physics is my reference point. Physicists didn't improve steam engines by trying a million engine designs. At some point thermodynamics came along and told you what's possible, what isn't, and why. I'd like something similar for neural networks: why scaling laws look the way they do, what representations models actually learn, when generalization happens and when it fails. Interpretability, phenomenology, small toy models where you can see the mechanism clearly.

AI can help there too, maybe a lot. It can propose hypotheses, find structure in training dynamics, discover symbolic formulas from data, check whether a story you tell about a model holds up. That's partly why I worked on things like KANs: I wanted models that are more interpretable, so that humans and AI can collaborate on understanding instead of treating the network as a black box.

So I'd put it this way. The coding-agent route asks how to make AI research faster. I'm more interested in how to make it deeper, so that what we learn is knowledge, not just a better checkpoint. Ideally the two meet. The agents give you scale, and the scientific understanding tells you where to point that scale. Without understanding, I worry recursive self-improvement looks more like recursive self-search: powerful, but somewhat blind.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts running more experiments with gaining deeper scientific understanding, but does not say that the desired approach increases the success rate of proposed ideas.

r002.rationale: It presents scale from agents and scientific understanding as complementary, but does not clearly frame execution diligence and intelligence as orthogonal dimensions.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that the coding-agent approach treats AI for AI as an engineering acceleration problem, and I'm more interested in it as a science problem.

What RSI Recursive and similar efforts are doing is essentially closing a loop: you take a strong model, give it a codebase, a benchmark, and compute, and let it propose and test changes to its own training pipeline, architecture, or data. The agent is the researcher, the loop is the lab, and the hope is that each iteration produces a slightly better agent, and the curve compounds. I respect this a lot. It's pragmatic, it's measurable, and frankly it's already producing real gains on things like kernel optimization and hyperparameter search. If your goal is to get to the frontier faster, this is a very reasonable bet.

But there's an assumption buried in it, which is that improvement can be found by searching within the space of things we already know how to write down. An agent editing a transformer training script is exploring a neighborhood around the current paradigm. It's very good at local hill-climbing. It's much less clear that it can tell you *why* the hill is shaped the way it is, or whether there's a different mountain altogether. When I look at the history of physics, the big jumps rarely came from running more experiments faster. They came from someone noticing a pattern across experiments and compressing it into a principle.

So the direction I want to pursue is closer to that second thing. I want AI to help us build a physics of AI, meaning understanding what neural networks are actually doing, in terms of a small number of concepts that generalize: how representations form, why scaling laws have the exponents they do, what the phase transitions during training correspond to, what makes something interpretable or not. My work on KANs, for instance, came from asking whether there's a different primitive than the neuron that is more aligned with how scientists actually think about functions. That's not something you discover by letting an agent tune a learning rate schedule. It comes from stepping back and asking a structural question.

The two directions aren't enemies. In fact, I think the recursive agent approach needs the science approach to avoid getting stuck. If your agent's search space is defined by today's abstractions, you will converge to a local optimum of today's abstractions. Understanding gives you new axes to search along. And conversely, I would love to use agents as tireless experimentalists for the science. Have them run thousands of controlled training runs, look for regularities, propose candidate laws, and let humans and models together do the compression step.

There's also a difference in what you consider the output. For the recursive self-improvement camp, the output is a better model. For me, the output is knowledge that a human can hold in their head. I care about that partly for safety reasons, because a system improving itself in ways nobody understands is not something I'm comfortable with, but mostly because I think understanding is what lets you make the next non-incremental move. If we end up with a superintelligent system and we still can't explain why a given architecture works, that feels like a strange kind of success to me.

So if I had to summarize it in one line: they're trying to make AI a faster engineer of AI. I'm trying to make AI a better scientist of AI. Speed is valuable. But I think, in the long run, insight is what compounds.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts faster engineering iteration with scientific understanding, but does not frame the difference as trying more ideas versus improving the success rate of proposed ideas.

r002.rationale: It says agents could run experiments while humans and models find laws, but does not present execution diligence and intelligence as orthogonal dimensions of improvement.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that a coding-agent approach starts with a concrete feedback loop: the agent writes code, runs it, evaluates the result, and uses that feedback to improve the system. That’s a powerful way to approach AI for AI, because many research ideas ultimately have to become working code.

The direction I’m more interested in is the research process around that loop. How does an AI decide which question is worth asking? Can it form a useful hypothesis, design an experiment that distinguishes between explanations, and revise its understanding when the result is surprising?

Coding is an essential part of that, but improving a metric and understanding why something works are different achievements. I’d like those to reinforce each other: better understanding should suggest better systems, and experiments with those systems should improve our understanding.

So I see these as complementary directions. The distinction is where you put the emphasis—on automating implementation and optimization, or on developing the scientific judgment that guides what to implement and why.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts automating implementation and optimization with scientific judgment, but does not frame the distinction as trying more ideas versus improving the success rate of proposed ideas.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes coding and optimization from understanding and scientific judgment, but does not present execution diligence and intelligence as orthogonal dimensions of improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
The distinction I would draw is between automating AI research as a workflow and improving our understanding of learning itself.

A coding agent can close a very useful loop: read code, propose a change, run an experiment, look at the metric, and iterate. My understanding of RSI Recursive’s approach is that it puts a lot of emphasis on making that loop increasingly autonomous. You can get substantial progress that way.

What interests me more is whether AI can help us discover the principles behind the results. Why does a particular architecture work? What structure has a model learned? Can we turn an empirical observation into a simple explanation that predicts what will happen in a new setting?

Those directions overlap, of course. You need coding and experiments to test an explanation. But the emphasis is different: are we primarily trying to produce a better-performing system, or are we trying to produce knowledge that makes the next system easier to understand and design? I’m more drawn to the second question.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts automating research experiments with understanding learning, but does not frame the distinction as trying more ideas versus improving the success rate of proposed ideas.

r002.rationale: It discusses autonomous execution and explanatory understanding as different emphases, but does not present execution diligence and intelligence as orthogonal dimensions of improvement.
